Although it was so brilliantly fine, with the blue sky powdered with gold, Miss Brill was glad that she had decided to wear her fur. <break time="0.8s" /> The air was perfectly still, but when she opened her mouth, there was just a faint chill, like the chill from a glass of iced water before you sip. <break time="0.8s" /> Great spots of light like white wine were splashed over the Jardins Publiques, the public gardens, and now and again a leaf came drifting down from the sky. <break time="0.8s" /> That afternoon she had taken the fur out of its box, shaken out the moth powder, and given it a good brush, feeling how nice it was to touch it again. <break time="0.8s" /> Then she had rubbed the life back into its dim little eyes, which seemed to ask her sadly, What has been happening to me. <break time="0.8s" /> Little rogue, she thought fondly as it bit its tail just by her left ear, and something light and sad, or rather something gentle, seemed to move in her heart. <break time="0.8s" /> There were a great many more people out this afternoon than last Sunday, and the band sounded louder and gayer because the Season had begun. <break time="0.8s" /> The conductor wore a new coat, and he flapped his arms like a rooster about to crow, while the bandsmen in the green rotunda blew out their cheeks.

Only two people shared her special seat, a fine old man in a velvet coat and a big old woman with a roll of knitting on her apron. <break time="0.8s" /> They did not speak, which was rather disappointing, for Miss Brill always looked forward to the conversation every Sunday. <break time="0.8s" /> She had become quite expert, she thought, at listening as though she did not listen, at sitting in other peoples lives just for a minute while they talked around her. <break time="0.8s" /> Last Sunday an Englishman in a dreadful Panama hat and his wife in button boots had sat there, and the wife had talked the whole time about spectacles. <break time="0.8s" /> She knew she needed them, but nothing her patient husband suggested could please her, and Miss Brill had wanted to shake her. <break time="0.8s" /> Now she watched the crowd, the couples and groups who were strolling to and fro, stopping to talk, to greet, and to buy flowers from an old beggar. <break time="0.8s" /> Little children ran among them, swooping and laughing, and when one small child suddenly fell down, its mother rushed to the rescue like a young hen. <break time="0.8s" /> Other people sat on the benches, but they were odd, silent, and nearly all old, as if they had just come from dark little rooms or even cupboards.
